newsitem.title: USA: Albright set to see world on inaugural trip.
newsitem.headline: Albright set to see world on inaugural trip.

text.p: New Secretary of State Madeleine Albright intends to get get right down to work on key foreign policy issues like NATO expansion with her first, globe-circling trip beginning Saturday, U.S. officials say.

After four years as U.N. ambassador, America's first female secretary of state already knows the government leaders and foreign ministers of most major countries and has planned a substantive agenda for her 11-day visit to Europe and Asia.
Normally, new U.S. secretaries of state limit their first overseas venture to Europe, home to America's oldest allies.

But Albright, who has quickly put her own stamp on the style, if not the substance, of the State Department, decided on an around-the-world extravaganza designed to emphasise that Asia, as well as Europe, is critical to U.S. interests.

"This is not a trip to introduce Madeleine Albright to these governments," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said of the journey that will take her to Rome, Bonn, Paris, Brussels, London, Moscow, Seoul, Tokyo and Beijing.

"It's a trip for her to roll up her sleeves and to get to work on the substance of our relationships with all these countries and to develop a coherent agenda with them and to press forward on the issues that are most important to us."

Albright expects to meet chiefs of state as well as her foreign minister colleagues, including Russian President Boris Yeltsin if he is able. Yeltsin has been recovering from a recent bout of pneumonia after heart surgery late last year.

In Europe, the overall focus is expected to be European security, including NATO expansion plans, internal reforms and alliance negotiations with Russia on a proposed charter defining a special relationship between old Cold War enemies.

NATO is to hold a summit in Madrid in July to invite east European nations once allied with Moscow to join its ranks. It is hoping to complete by then a charter spelling out ties with Russia too. But Moscow opposes NATO expansion and in recent days the rhetoric of Russian critics has heated up notably.

Concerns about the Bosnia peace deal, Turkey's trend toward Islamic fundamentalism, Greek-Turkish tensions over Cyprus and reviving Israeli-Syria peace talks could also come up in Albright's meetings.
In addition, there are bilateral issues to contend with, including recent U.S.-German tensions over Bonn's treatment of Scientologists and peace efforts in Northern Ireland.
Britain's Northern Ireland secretary, Patrick Mayhew, on Thursday dismissed media reports he was being snubbed by Albright in a policy dispute over Northern Ireland.

U.S. officials have denied British press reports that President Bill Clinton is shifting his policy to take a harder line towards the Nationalist Sinn Fein party after the end of a ceasefire by its military wing, the Irish Republican Army.
In Asia, there is not the same broad regional security issue that NATO is for Europe. But the agenda is still full.
Albright is expected to discuss with Seoul U.S.-South Korean efforts to work with North Korea under a 1994 agreement that froze Pyongyang's nuclear programme.

The two allies have proposed four-party talks, including China, aimed at forging a permanent peace on the peninsula, divided since the 1950-53 Korean war. But Pyongyang has resisted the talks and there are tensions between Seoul and Washington over what and how many gestures -- such as food aid -- should be extended to woo North Korea's support.

Some U.S. officials were cool to an Albright visit to China because her predecessor, Warren Christopher, was just there in November and an outline of high-level exchange visits for 1997 had been set. The first was to be a Washington visit by China's foreign minister.

But Albright decided that, given China's importance, she had to stop there. The visit comes as she is considering whether to recommend U.S. sponsorship of a U.N. resolution criticising Beijing's deteriorating human rights record.

There are also continuing U.S. concerns over China's arms and technology transfers, but a bright spot is Beijing's signal it is willing to drop many of its biggest trade barriers to win membership in the World Trade Organisation.
